I then proceeded to the sales floor and located the multi-deck refrigeration system. The case temperature was elevated, with the case temperature at 42°F. I began troubleshooting System #7 and found that the unit was locked out on a high-discharge-pressure safety trip. I checked the discharge pressure and found it operating at approximately 330 PSI. I then verified the discharge pressure safety control and found it set to cut out at 400 PSI. Next, I inspected the condenser coil and found no visible obstructions; however, the condenser fins were damaged in several areas. I also checked the liquid line filter drier for any signs of restriction and found none. After power-cycling the controller to restart the system, the unit tripped again on high discharge pressure. I then performed a thorough cleaning of the condenser coil until the rinse water ran clear. Once cleaning was completed, I restarted the system and monitored operation. After cleaning, the system operated normally and did not trip on high discharge pressure.

Then, I installed service ports on the liquid line dryers and the suction fill-up spot on the compressor for both circuits. The blast chiller operates on two circuits. I took the unit out of a defrost the temps went up to about 17 degrees then started dropping again
Unit is now working and there are no more alarms present
If there is another issue I recommend changing out the filter drier

E7BBF418-6B8A-4636-BE72-2E8CBE32A27D.root_cause: Found a fuse blown. Had to source new fuse as it is not a common style fuse (age of unit). Got the blower motor up and running. Called Tunilabs back to put unit into test, found that the controller would run it in Free-cool, but not turn compressor on. Went through all electrical transformers, and contactor coils to ensure no other issues. Ran continuity test through both safeties and oil control up to the contactor, safeties are good to go. With the temps in the low to mid 30°s there is something holding out control voltage, either a freeze stat on the evap coil, one of the multiple controllers due to ambient temp. Also getting the unit properly charged in these temps would not work. Will need to do more testing when the weather is warmer, spring PM. Traced the issue back to 2 blown 15amp fuses that energize the transformer that powers up the control circuit. Once new fuses were installed, got comms back up. Called Tunilabs again and had the unit forced into cool, still got no control voltage. Again traced the wiring back to the Bellimo module that would not power up. This module sends control voltage through the correct pathways for either cool/heat. Found that there was no power getting through the control circuit at all. Nothing to the compressor module, nothing to through the safeties, no voltage out of electrical box at all other than primary voltage. Will need to return with another tech to sort out the wiring as it is been modified/re wired over the years and no wire numbers put on the modified wiring. Likely culprit is the Bellimo module, the RTCR board or the relay board. Will have to remove the larger panels to properly check the wiring. Whatever took out those fuses likely shorted something else in the control circuit. Started with tracing out voltage drop to Belimo controller, traced it back to a fuse holder connector. Then began tracing control voltage to compressor 1 contactor. This brought us to the old style relay board, found missing relays, bad relays and some creative wiring already in place. After a few wiring adjustments we were able to get the compressor contactor active when called for cooling. Next we wired in the hi/low safeties, oil pressure safety. This piece of equipment needs 3 things to make it work. 1) water in the de-superheater/ Evap-a/way pan. 2) factory rated air flow across condensing unit. It is undersized and even a small amount of dirt causes the compressor to overheat. 3) Enriched sub cooler at evaporator. I had to cool the compressor’s discharge gas temperature by adding ice to the de-superheater pan. I had to clean the honeycombs and condenser coil again, just like last time. And I had to set superheat on the TXV at the outlet of the sub cooler. Liquid refrigerant was so hot by the time it hit the sub cooler that it did nothing to cool the liquid and nothing to cool the compressor. Over enriched the TXV to compensate for high operating temperatures. Set superheat at outlet of the sub cooler. Dropped operating pressure by 30#s by balancing case operation. *This case needs monthly PM service to keep it running. It’s location next to the front door and service counter make it a high traffic area that requires more attention. Poor housekeeping. The unit is parked next to the front door which affects liquid line temp and discharge temps. Poor placement of the unit is the cause of all of this.

Compressor 3 still tripping on oil failure and not feeding oil. Found both the oil pickup screen and inlet screen plugged up. Cleaned both screens and compressor is feeding oil properly. It is likely that all the oil screens on Rack A are very dirty. Oil coming out of the compressor is black. Recommend full rack oil change, as well as changing oil filter and filter driers. On arrival found only comp 1 running on rack a. 3,4,5 off on oil fail. Frosting on oil differential valve. Pumped down and pulled apart debris in valve metering oil. Also checked inlet screens for comp 3,4,5. 3 clean from previous cleaning. 4,5 were dirty cleaned and reassembled took vaccine and got rack back online. While pulling down differential valve clogged again. Pulled apart cleaned. Watched all systems come to temp. Even though we are waiting on compressor we should do full oil change/ oil differential sooner as there may be more debris inside top half of valve we cannot clean.

8309EC6C-52AF-4CA8-AC68-BE6D08969CB1.root_cause: Verified the defrost circuit and found the line voltage defrost breaker had failed, preventing proper power from being supplied to the defrost circuit. Replaced the failed line voltage breaker and retested circuit operation. During operational checks, determined the defrost circuit was still not energizing correctly. Continued troubleshooting and traced the fault to a failed defrost contactor with defective contacts preventing voltage from passing through the circuit under load. A suitable replacement contactor was not available on-site and will need to be sourced before repairs can be completed. Once the correct contactor is obtained, it will need to be installed to restore proper defrost circuit operation. Returned to site following replacement of the failed line voltage defrost breaker and restoration of the defrost control circuit. Verified proper operation of the replacement breaker and confirmed the defrost contactor is energizing and switching correctly. Performed additional diagnostics on the evaporator defrost circuit and isolated the remaining fault to an open top coil heater. Confirmed the upper coil heater has failed electrically and will require replacement. The lower coil heater remains operational, allowing the case to continue completing defrost cycles and maintain acceptable operation.

When testing the compressor with load i get a very high current ( 120A) , compared to when it has not load ( 8A) The diagnostic is either bad winding ( for higher voltage) or a shortened motor. Confirmed the new compressor is bad.

Observed significant frost accumulation on the suction line consistent with evaporator floodback. Diagnosed failed suction line temperature sensor producing erroneous superheat calculations. Returned to troubleshoot Case A16B and identified an incorrectly sized SPW-2 valve cartridge contributing to excessive refrigerant feed, suction line frosting, and floodback conditions. 0A92CDBC-3D27-40E5-81C2-6520B1723A85.root_cause: Only issue I found was stage five compressor on rack A was off on run proof. Reset high-pressure control compressor turned on no other issues at this time.

72228274-5C77-4F97-8E0C-45CF673D52E5.root_cause: Found Blower motor overload (Schneider LRD-35) control contacts stuck open. Found VFD frequency on L2 load side imbalanced by +40% from L1 and L3. This is what damaged the integrity of the blower motor windings and eventually blew the fuse on L2. Found that existing VFD FLA are rated for 31 amps and blower motor is rated for 29.5 amps indicating that VFD is undersized for this drive motor. Recommending that a 30hp 40 FLA VFD is installed to ensure that drive does not operate at more then 70% of its FLA guarantee that drive will live long healthy life (approximately 30+ years). Found that control wiring for blower motor overload (LRD-35) was positioned in the control circuit after the time delay relay for the bypass contactor, causing the overload not to protect the motor in VFD operations, in turn allowing the VFD to damage the motor when the VFD failed. Re-wired overload to be in play and protect the blower motor from over amping whether it’s in VFD or Bypass operations.

The gaskets must be replaced so the doors close properly and ice does not accumulate; photos of the required parts are attached. Required parts: 5 gaskets, 1x 3090935KT (Innovator Door Bottom Socket Kit), 1x 3090933KT (Innovator Door Top Hinge Kit), 1x HATF9042AAG240 relay, 1x HAT903CSAC 220 relay.

I then achieved a 6°F superheat and the left case successfully pulled down to temperature and began cycling normally. I disassembled the right case as necessary and replaced the faulty case temperature sensor. After installation, I verified the new sensor in an ice bath and confirmed it was reading 32°F. After allowing the case to run, the right case began cycling normally and maintaining proper temperature. We will return. Returned to site. Spoke with Dennis and Josh and we all agreed to replace the TXV on the left deli case. I pumped down the circuit. I unbraized the filter drier and the old txv. Braized in a new filter drier and new txv body. Installed a cartridge and power head on the txv. Placed circuit in a vacuum. After vacuum I opened system and let cases drop down in temp. Took a while to dial in superheat on new tvx. This case is now showing 37 degrees and cycling on and off. The case on the right I had to play with and keep adjusting the txv as well. 6C8EAE8F-9E40-476D-9433-3025977F7403.root_cause: Found that the case temperature would not pull below 45°F. Verified evaporator fan motor operation and confirmed the fan was rotating in the correct direction. Checked thermostat operation and verified it was properly cycling the compressor on and off. Connected gauges to the service ports at the condensing unit and found the system was low on refrigerant. Performed a leak search using an electronic leak detector and leak detection bubbles. Located a refrigerant leak at the suction service valve. When attempting to remove the service port cap, refrigerant immediately began leaking from the valve. Attempted to remove the top cap of the suction king valve to inspect the valve stem position and determine if it was partially seated, allowing refrigerant to escape. The cap was severely rusted and seized. Applied WD-40 and cleaned the area with sandpaper in an attempt to free the cap; however, it would not loosen. Excessive force could not be applied without risking damage to the suction line. Will need to order and replace the leaking suction king valve. Once the replacement valve is on site, return visit will be required to recover refrigerant as needed, replace the valve, pressure test the system with nitrogen, perform a complete leak check, evacuate the system, and recharge with refrigerant. Cleaned up work area and documented findings with pictures and notes. System is currently operating at approximately 50% capacity. Return visit required once parts are received. Compressor energized but was not pumping refrigerant. Verified voltage and found the overload protector tripping due to excessive compressor temperature. Allowed the compressor to cool using a bag of ice and attempted to restart after it had completely cooled, but the compressor still would not pump. Verified all electrical components were operating properly, confirming a failed compressor, most likely caused by operating without refrigerant. Disconnected power to the unit to prevent store personnel from plugging it back in and causing additional damage. Unit is 100% down. Recommend do not plug in or attempt to operate until compressor is replaced. Office to order replacement compressor.

41626F10-B6A0-4456-8379-FCE982DE6AD4.root_cause: Inspection revealed frost accumulation around the TXV and liquid line components. Superheat readings were elevated and unstable, indicating the evaporator was being starved of refrigerant. Further evaluation identified a temperature drop across the liquid line filter drier consistent with a restriction. The restricted filter drier is limiting liquid refrigerant flow to the TXV, resulting in reduced evaporator feed and poor case pull-down performance. TXV operation was evaluated by making adjustments and monitoring system response. Although temporary changes in suction pressure and superheat were observed, the valve failed to maintain consistent refrigerant control and continued to underfeed the evaporator. Findings indicate a restricted liquid line filter drier and a failed TXV requiring replacement. Further troubleshooting found a restricted liquid line ball valve on circuit 2.2. Pumped the circuit down, replaced the valve, and restored liquid flow. Solid liquid was confirmed at the evaporator, but the TXV failed to modulate properly, indicating an internal failure.

Under further investigation, I determined there had been a planned power outage. The compressors remained energized while the condenser fan motors lost power, causing excessive head pressure to build until the relief valve opened. Once power was fully restored, I brought the rack back online and verified proper operation. I then added 75 lbs of R-407A refrigerant to restore the receiver level to 20%. After charging the system, I monitored operation and verified that all cases reached and maintained proper setpoint temperatures. I also verified that the rack was maintaining proper suction pressure. I ended up brazing it unconventional style since the elbows are paper thin. Pulled deep vacuum on that half of condenser. Performed decay negative pressure test. Performed positive pressure test. Put back into circulation. Added 25 lbs of refrigerant. Added one gallon of oil. All of rack b is back up and functioning. Verified all temps came down to set point.

So at that moment, I thought bad transducer then close my valve and remove the transducer and went to my van to get another transducer. I installed the new transducer and opened my valve back up. I then checked my pressure and my pressure was still reading the same as the original transducer. So I did cut the wire connecting the transducer to the controller and made a new wire connection. After making the new wire connection, of the controller still read the same pressure as before. So I started to read the manual, learn how to use the controller, and called RDM for assistance on the programming for the controller. Unfortunately, RDM tech-support could not login to the 594 H-E-B location. Through the process of RDM tech support walking through the procedure, the case controller program was removed from 3 out of 4 controllers on the meat case. So I continue to look into my controller and figure out what P5 meant and why am I transducer was reading a different pressure for my gauges. I compared the controller from the case I was working on to the case that was in operational condition. After going through the parameters and comparing the two case controllers, I came to the conclusion that the case I was working on had the complete wrong parameters. So I went through each parameter and took notes on the difference between the two cases. I’ve been started to reprogram this case through the case controller.

E31632ED-ECB1-40B4-A76B-01E1C6DE0ABD.root_cause: Found no water flow from supply. Inspected Belimo actuator and found valve spring-returned closed due to power interruption. Suspect improper valve operation caused weak water supply and incomplete saturation of fill media, reducing adiabatic efficiency and contributing to repeated high gas cooler/max pressure alarms, potential relief events, and low liquid alarms. Verified control signal and confirmed 2 VDC is command to fully open and 10 VDC to fully closed in this application. Tested actuator by removing power and found valve failing open, which does not match system logic. Suspect actuator was indexed incorrectly and operating in reverse. Adjusted actuator by reversing polarity to fail-closed configuration to match 2–10 VDC control logic. Confirmed signal and feedback not matching and confirmed strong water flow with full saturation of media pads during demand.

8E7325F6-2287-4F2C-9A10-4D19F16C398A.root_cause: Dairy walk in cooler REDA11 has 2/4 evaporators that have bad EEV coils. Magnets placed on valves by previous tech.  Coils not available locally . This method, used as an emergency temporary fix, works in many instances. In this rare case it flooded compressors and  they tripped on discharge pressure. Without EEV coils available the two evaporators will not hold proper temperature, they will maintain in the high 40’s, 48-49 degrees; too warm . Magnets are needed to force EEV’s open. A solution is to install liquid line ball valves at each evaporator that has bad EEV coils , Evaporators REDA11c and 11d. Ball valves can be closed a certain percentage to regulate flow of refrigerant. Pumped down entire dairy circuit. Installed ball valves. Vacuum pulled. Opened up refrigeration. Leak searched. No leaks . After adjusting ball valves in small increments determined that they needed to be opened only 1/8 of a turn . Anything greater would cause liquid refrigerant to flood compressors at Rack. After monitoring rack and line temperatures all 4 evaporators at 36-37 degrees.
